title: William James
orientation: This chapter treats William James (1842-1910), the psychologist-philosopher who became the recognized leader of American philosophy, on two fronts: his 'radical empiricism,' which denies that the relation of subject (knower) to object (known) is fundamental, and his 'pragmatism' (with its forerunner, the 'will to believe'), which redefines truth in terms of an idea's practical, satisfying effects. Russell endorses the first doctrine but mounts a sustained, multi-pronged attack on the second, treating it as intellectually confused and, in its application to religion, as a symptom of a dangerous 'subjectivistic madness' in modern philosophy.
historical_background: James was a New Englander from a Puritan background whose warm, democratic, unsnobbish temperament Russell contrasts with the aristocratic, aesthetic Catholicism of his philosophical rival George Santayana. James's study of medicine gave him materialist leanings that his strong religious feeling held in check. Russell notes James was one of three chief protagonists of pragmatism (with F. C. S. Schiller and John Dewey, treated in the following chapter), and that the movement's principle was first stated by C. S. Peirce.
philosophical_problems: Is the distinction between subject (knower) and object (known) fundamental to reality, or derivative from something more basic?
What is the single 'stuff' of which mind and matter are both composed, if the subject-object dualism is rejected?
Are we ever entitled to believe something on insufficient evidence, particularly in religious matters?
What does it mean for a belief or idea to be 'true' -- correspondence to fact, or beneficial practical effects?
Can the pragmatist definition of truth survive being applied consistently to statements about the past and to religious belief?

philosophers_discussed.name: William James
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The chapter's sole primary subject. Russell expounds and largely endorses James's doctrine of radical empiricism and 'pure experience,' then expounds and sharply criticizes James's 'will to believe' and his pragmatist redefinition of truth.

philosophers_discussed.name: George Santayana
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Presented as James's temperamental opposite: a 'Catholic free-thinker' who appreciated religion aesthetically and historically without belief in its dogmas, an attitude James (whose doctor's thesis Santayana had called 'the perfection of rottenness') regarded as immoral.

philosophers_discussed.name: C. S. Peirce
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Credited by James as the original source of the pragmatist principle: that to attain clarity about an object we need only consider its conceivable practical effects.

philosophers_discussed.name: F. C. S. Schiller
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named as one of the three protagonists of pragmatism alongside James and Dewey, but noted by Russell to be of lesser importance than the other two.

philosophers_discussed.name: John Dewey
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Mentioned as the third major pragmatist, whose more scientifically oriented version of the doctrine Russell says he will examine in the next chapter, contrasted with James's religiously and morally oriented emphasis.

core_concepts.name: Radical empiricism and 'pure experience'
core_concepts.plain_explanation: James argues that the everyday assumption that there is a 'knower' (mind) on one side and a 'known' (object) on the other is not basic to reality. Instead, there is just one kind of raw material, 'pure experience,' and any given piece of it can count as either a knower or a known thing depending on the context in which we consider it.
core_concepts.precise_definition: First published in the 1904 essay 'Does "Consciousness" Exist?', James's doctrine that the subject-object relation is not fundamental: consciousness 'is the name of a nonentity' with 'no aboriginal stuff or quality of being' distinct from that of material objects; there is instead 'only one primal stuff or material,' called 'pure experience' and defined as 'the immediate flux of life which furnishes the material to our later reflection,' out of which knowing arises as a derivative relation between two portions of that stuff.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell states he was persuaded by James (and those who agreed with him) to abandon his own earlier view and now regards this as correct, calling it grounds by itself for giving James 'a high place among philosophers'; it undercuts almost the whole traditional apparatus of mind/matter dualism, the contemplative ideal, and the traditional notion of truth.
core_concepts.historical_origin: First published in the essay 'Does "Consciousness" Exist?' (1904).
examples: "Consciousness... is the name of a nonentity, and has no right to a place among first principles."
A given undivided portion of experience can be, in one context, a knower, and in another, something known.
objections: Russell disputes only James's use of the word 'experience': common sense holds that many things occur (e.g., events on the far side of the moon) without being experienced by anyone, so 'experience' cannot be coextensive with the 'stuff' of the world.
Russell suggests James's phrase 'pure experience' points to 'a perhaps unconscious Berkeleian idealism' that James himself never squarely confronted.
competing_positions: The traditional dualist view, assumed by 'almost everything in accepted philosophy,' that a knower (mind or soul) is aware of a separate object known
Berkeley's and Hegel's view that what is not experienced is nothing, which Russell (with most philosophers) holds invalid
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly gives rise to the doctrine Russell calls 'neutral monism,' further developed in the final chapter on logical analysis in connection with modern physics and psychology.

core_concepts.name: Neutral monism
core_concepts.plain_explanation: If mind and matter are not two different kinds of stuff, but experience shows up sometimes as a 'knower' and sometimes as a 'known,' then the world's basic material is neither mental nor physical -- it is 'neutral,' prior to that distinction.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine, advocated by James's followers though not developed by James himself, that the material of which the world is constructed is neither mind nor matter but something anterior to both, following from radical empiricism's abolition of the subject-object dualism as a distinction of 'stuff.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It offers a way to dissolve the traditional mind-matter problem at its root, rather than solving it within the old dualist framework.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Drawn as an implication of James's 1904 essay by those who agreed with him, though James himself did not draw it out.
core_concepts.associated_philosopher: William James (doctrine developed by his followers)
competing_positions: James's own apparent, if unintended, drift toward Berkeleian idealism
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell connects it directly to the mind-matter theory he develops in the closing chapter on logical analysis, where physics and psychology are said to be converging on treating both mind and matter as 'convenient ways of grouping events.'

core_concepts.name: The Will to Believe
core_concepts.plain_explanation: James argues that in matters (especially religious ones) where the evidence is not conclusive either way, but where a decision cannot be avoided even by doing nothing, we have a right to choose to believe -- because avoiding error is not more important than believing truth, and refusing to decide risks missing out on truths a bolder person would have believed.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Published in 1896, James's doctrine that the duty of veracity consists of two coequal precepts, 'believe truth' and 'shun error,' and that since the sceptic wrongly privileges only the second, a person facing a forced, momentous, and evidentially undecidable option (paradigmatically religious belief) is entitled to adopt a believing attitude even though 'our merely logical intellect may not have been coerced.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It was, in Russell's account, a transitional doctrine leading naturally to pragmatism's redefinition of truth, and functioned as James's defence of the right to religious belief in an age of scientific scepticism.
core_concepts.historical_origin: The Will to Believe (1896); Russell compares its underlying attitude to that of Rousseau's Savoyard vicar.
examples: The stranger-on-the-train example: not knowing a stranger's name, positive veracity might seem to license believing he is called 'Ebenezer Wilkes Smith' rather than merely suspending judgement.
objections: Russell: James never once mentions probability, yet almost every real question admits of some assessment of relative probability, which collapses the 'equal right to believe' argument (illustrated with a Chinese observer choosing among Confucianism, Buddhism, and Christianity, which cannot all be true).

Russell: James wrongly treats belief and disbelief as the only alternatives, ignoring the intermediate, common and rational state of acting on a working hypothesis while remaining open to further evidence.

Russell's own precept of veracity: give any hypothesis worth considering exactly the degree of credence the evidence warrants, and seek further evidence when the question is important -- 'plain common sense,' and 'quite different' from James's procedure.
competing_positions: Russell's evidentialist account of veracity (proportion belief to evidence)
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Develops, in Russell's account, into James's full pragmatist theory of truth published in 1907.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Chiefly a defence of the right to religious belief in the absence of conclusive theoretical grounds.

core_concepts.name: Pragmatist theory of truth
core_concepts.plain_explanation: James claims an idea is 'true' not because it matches some fact, but because believing it is useful -- it helps us get along well with the rest of our experience. So truth is a kind of practical payoff rather than a copy of reality.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Set out in Pragmatism, a New Name for Some Old Ways of Thinking (1907), James's doctrine that 'an idea is "true" so long as to believe it is profitable to our lives,' that truth is 'made' by events rather than discovered, that 'to agree' with reality means being guided usefully toward it rather than 'copying' it, and that 'the "true" is only the expedient in the way of our thinking... in the long run and on the whole.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is James's central, most distinctive philosophical contribution and the doctrine, in Russell's judgment, on which James's reputation as a serious epistemologist most depends -- and also the doctrine Russell finds most objectionable, especially in its application to religion ('if the hypothesis of God works satisfactorily... it is true').
core_concepts.historical_origin: Pragmatism, a New Name for Some Old Ways of Thinking (1907), building on the principle first enunciated by C. S. Peirce.
examples: "We cannot reject any hypothesis if consequences useful to life flow from it."
"If the hypothesis of God works satisfactorily in the widest sense of the word, it is true."
objections: Russell's regress objection: judging a belief's consequences to be good is itself only 'true' if that judgement has good consequences, and so on ad infinitum -- 'obviously this won't do.'

Russell's Columbus example: to know whether Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492 we would, on James's theory, have to weigh the ethical and practical effects of believing 1492 versus 1491 or 1493, rather than simply consulting historical causes -- an 'incredible complication.'

Russell's causes-versus-effects objection: a statement like 'there was such a person as Columbus' is true because of a real man who lived 450 years ago (its causes), not because of the effects of believing it.

Russell's Santa Claus reductio: since belief in Santa Claus 'works satisfactorily in the widest sense of the word,' James's definition would make 'Santa Claus exists' true although Santa Claus does not exist.
competing_positions: Russell's own causal theory of truth: a belief about a past occurrence is true, or as near true as possible, in virtue of a certain relation to its causes, not its future effects
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Contrasted by Russell with John Dewey's related but distinct 'instrumentalism,' examined in the following chapter.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Applied by James directly to religious belief; Russell notes the Pope condemned this 'pragmatic defence of religion,' and argues it reduces God to a useful hypothesis rather than an actual being.

core_concepts.name: 'Experience' and its limits
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Russell asks what actually distinguishes an experienced event from an unexperienced one, concluding that experience requires life and, more specifically, that an event is 'experienced' when it sets up a habit (memory being one kind of habit).
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's own supplementary analysis, offered in assessing James's use of 'experience': there is no experience except where there is life, but experience is not coextensive with life either, since many things happen to an organism without being noticed; an event may be said to be 'experienced' when it sets up a habit, habits being possible only in living organisms (illustrated by the burnt child who fears fire even without explicit memory of being burnt).
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It grounds Russell's sole substantive disagreement with James's radical empiricism, and shows why Russell thinks 'pure experience' cannot, after all, be identified with the single 'stuff' of the whole world.
examples: Rain falling in an uninhabited desert is not experienced, though rain seen or felt to fall is.
A burnt poker does not fear the fire, however often it is heated, because it cannot form habits.

arguments.title: James's argument against the subject-object dualism
premises: Traditional philosophy assumes a fundamental relation of 'knowing' in which a subject (mind) is aware of a distinct object.
But no 'aboriginal stuff or quality of being' distinguishes the material out of which thoughts are made from that of which material objects are made.
There is only one primal stuff, 'pure experience,' and knowing is a particular relation between two portions of it.
arguments.conclusion: The subject-object relation is not fundamental but derivative; a given portion of experience can function as knower in one context and as known in another.
arguments.explanation: James denies that he is rejecting the function of knowing itself, only the view that 'consciousness' names a special kind of entity or 'thing' distinct from what is known; this clears the ground for neutral monism.
objections: Russell accepts the conclusion, but questions James's use of 'experience' as the name for the single underlying stuff, since not everything that exists is experienced.
implications: Undermines the traditional dualism of mind and matter, the contemplative ideal, and the traditional notion of truth, all of which Russell says 'need to be radically reconsidered' if the argument succeeds.

arguments.title: The Will to Believe argument
premises: The duty of veracity consists of two coequal precepts: believe truth, and shun error.
The sceptic wrongly attends only to the second precept, and so fails to believe various truths a less cautious person would believe.
In matters (like religion) where no adequate theoretical grounds for decision exist, even inaction is itself a decision.
arguments.conclusion: We have a right, in such forced and undecidable cases, to adopt a believing attitude, even though our 'merely logical intellect' has not been coerced by evidence.
arguments.explanation: James's argument turns on treating belief and disbelief as symmetrical risks (dupery through hope versus dupery through fear) rather than treating suspension of judgement as generally preferable when evidence is lacking.
objections: Russell: the argument ignores probability, which is almost always discoverable and which, once admitted, defeats the claim that mutually exclusive hypotheses (e.g., rival religions) can each be believed with equal right.
Russell: the argument wrongly assumes only full belief or full disbelief are available, ignoring degrees of credence and hypothesis-testing.
implications: If sound, licenses religious and other beliefs adopted without conclusive evidence; if Russell's objections stand, the argument collapses once probability and degrees of belief are properly considered.

arguments.title: The pragmatist argument for truth as beneficial effect
premises: Ideas become true insofar as they help us get into satisfactory relations with other parts of our experience.
'Agreeing' with reality does not mean copying it, but being usefully guided toward it or put into good working contact with it.
Our obligation to seek truth is part of our general obligation to do what pays.
arguments.conclusion: 'The "true" is only the expedient in the way of our thinking... in the long run and on the whole'; a belief (including belief in God) is true if it works satisfactorily.
arguments.explanation: James treats truth as one species of the good rather than a separate category, and as something that 'happens' to an idea and is 'made' true by events, rather than as a fixed relation to antecedent fact.
objections: Russell's regress: whether a belief's effects are 'good' is itself only 'true' if judging it so has good effects, ad infinitum.
Russell's causal counter-theory: true beliefs about the past (e.g., that Columbus existed) are true because of their causes (real past events), not their future effects.

Russell's Santa Claus and Hitler reductios: the definition would make useful false beliefs 'true,' which is absurd, since asserting that something exists is not the same as asserting that believing it exists is beneficial.
implications: Applied to religion, dissolves the question of whether God actually exists into the question of whether belief in God is beneficial -- which Russell says the genuine believer, unlike James, would never accept as an adequate account of what they mean by 'God exists.'

key_distinctions: Subject/object (knower/known) as fundamental vs. as a derivative relation between portions of 'pure experience'
Dualism of mind and matter vs. neutral monism (a single, neutral underlying stuff)
Believing truth vs. shunning error, as the two (allegedly coequal) precepts of veracity
Truth as correspondence/copying of reality vs. truth as beneficial practical effect ('the expedient in our thinking')
Truth judged by causes (what made a belief arise) vs. truth judged by effects (what results from holding it)
Genuine belief in God as an actual being vs. James's 'belief in belief in God' on account of its good effects
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell compares James's Will to Believe to the attitude of Rousseau's Savoyard vicar, and traces the pragmatist principle to C. S. Peirce. He contrasts James's Protestant, democratic, morally earnest religiosity with the aesthetic, historically minded Catholic free-thinking of Santayana, framing this as a persistent temperamental opposition surviving among the unorthodox.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell explicitly defers fuller treatment of pragmatism's more scientific variant to John Dewey, discussed in the next chapter, noting the difference of emphasis between James's religious/moral concerns and Dewey's scientific ones. James's radical empiricism and neutral monism are picked up again in the closing chapter on logical analysis, where Russell connects them to developments in modern physics and psychology.
political_social_context: James's philosophy reflects his New England Puritan and democratic background; his insistence that there cannot be 'one truth for philosophers and another for the vulgar' is presented by Russell as flowing from this democratic temperament, in contrast to Santayana's more aristocratic, aesthetic sensibility.
religion_science_culture_context: James's philosophy is shaped by the tension between the materialist tendencies instilled by his medical training and his strong Protestant religious feeling; Russell notes that the Pope formally condemned the pragmatic defence of religion that James's doctrine of truth seemed to offer.
russell_presentation: Russell divides his treatment sharply in two. He first expounds James's radical empiricism at length and states plainly that he has come to agree with it: the subject-object relation is not fundamental, and 'pure experience' (though Russell disputes James's use of that particular word) underlies both knower and known. He then turns to the Will to Believe and pragmatism, which he treats as intellectually indefensible despite acknowledging their psychological and religious appeal. Using the examples of a stranger's name, Columbus's voyage, and belief in Santa Claus or God, Russell argues that James's definition of truth as beneficial effect leads to absurdities, ignores probability, and, applied to religion, substitutes belief in God for God himself -- 'only a form of the subjectivistic madness which is characteristic of most modern philosophy,' in Russell's closing judgment.
critical_context: Common scholarly assessment: James's radical empiricism and 'neutral monism' are usually judged his most durable technical contributions, anticipating later 'no-ownership' and process-oriented accounts of mind, while his pragmatist theory of truth is widely regarded (including by many pragmatists themselves) as needing significant refinement to avoid the kind of circularity and conflation-of-truth-with-verification objections Russell raises here; later pragmatists distinguished more carefully between an idea's being true and its being verified or found useful, partly in response to criticisms of exactly this kind.
key_takeaways: William James was central to American philosophy on two fronts: radical empiricism (rejecting subject-object dualism) and pragmatism (redefining truth as beneficial effect).

Russell endorses James's radical empiricism -- that pure experience, not a subject-object dualism, is fundamental -- while disputing only James's identification of 'experience' with the whole stuff of the world.
Radical empiricism's 'neutral monism,' though not developed by James himself, holds the basic stuff of the world is neither mind nor matter.

James's Will to Believe argues we may adopt belief without conclusive evidence in forced, momentous choices (especially religious ones); Russell objects that it ignores probability and degrees of belief.

James's pragmatism defines truth as an idea's beneficial practical effect rather than its correspondence to fact; Russell attacks this with a regress objection and examples (Columbus, Santa Claus, God) showing it can make useful falsehoods 'true.'
Russell's own view is that a belief about the past is true or false in virtue of its causes, not its future effects -- the reverse of James's position.
study_notes:
This chapter is best read as two separate arguments joined by one man. In the first, Russell is an ally: work through why he thinks the ordinary picture of a 'knower' inspecting a separate 'known object' can be replaced by a single kind of stuff (experience) that plays different roles in different contexts -- and notice that Russell's only real complaint is about the word 'experience' itself, since he thinks unexperienced events (like the far side of the moon) still exist. That objection is worth dwelling on, since it shows Russell trying to save James's insight about subject and object while rejecting an idealist reading of it.

In the second argument, Russell is an opponent, and it pays to separate three distinct moves he makes against pragmatism: (1) the probability objection to the Will to Believe -- that James ignores relative likelihoods, so his 'equal right to believe' collapses once you realize rival, mutually exclusive hypotheses cannot all be equally likely; (2) the regress objection to pragmatist truth -- judging a belief's effects 'good' is itself only true if that judgement has good effects, forever; and (3) the causes-versus-effects objection -- our ordinary reason for calling a historical claim true (like 'Columbus existed') is a fact about the past, not a calculation about the future usefulness of believing it. The Santa Claus and God examples are Russell's way of making objection (3) vivid: if only effects matter, useful falsehoods become 'true,' which he regards as absurd and, applied to religion, as replacing a real object of worship with a psychologically comforting habit of believing.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: James's view that the split between 'the mind that knows' and 'the object known' isn't basic to reality -- there's just one kind of raw material, experience, that can play either role.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: James's 1904 doctrine denying that the subject-object relation is fundamental, holding instead that there is only one primal stuff ('pure experience') out of which both knowers and known objects are constituted, knowing being a derivative relation between two portions of that stuff.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: James's name for the single basic 'stuff' the whole world is made of, before it gets sorted into 'mind' and 'matter.'
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Defined by James as 'the immediate flux of life which furnishes the material to our later reflection'; the single primal stuff of radical empiricism, out of which the subject-object relation derivatively arises.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that the basic 'stuff' of the universe is neither mental nor physical, but something more basic that can show up as either.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A doctrine developed by James's followers (not James himself) as an implication of radical empiricism: reality is composed of a single kind of neutral material, anterior to the mind/matter distinction.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: James's claim that when evidence can't settle a big, unavoidable question (like religion), we're entitled to just choose to believe.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: James's 1896 doctrine that the duty of veracity comprises two coequal precepts ('believe truth' and 'shun error'), licensing a believing attitude in forced, momentous, evidentially undecidable options even without intellectual coercion by evidence.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The theory that an idea is 'true' if believing it works out well for you, rather than because it matches some fact.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: James's 1907 doctrine that truth is 'made' by events and consists in an idea's being 'profitable to our lives'; 'agreement' with reality means being usefully guided by it, not copying it.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A related idea developed by John Dewey, discussed in the next chapter, that substitutes for 'truth' the notion of a belief being justified by present evidence for future action.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Not James's own term, but flagged here as the concept explored fully in the following chapter's contrast between James's and Dewey's versions of pragmatism.

questions.prompt: What does James mean by 'pure experience,' and what philosophical dualism is it meant to replace?
questions.answer: 'Pure experience' is James's name for the single primal 'stuff' out of which everything, including both knowers and known objects, is composed; it replaces the traditional dualism of subject (mind/knower) and object (thing known), which James denies is fundamental.
questions.explanation: This is the core claim of James's 1904 essay 'Does "Consciousness" Exist?', which Russell says persuaded him to change his own earlier view.

questions.prompt: Which philosopher said, 'The prince of darkness may be a gentleman, as we are told he is, but whatever the God of earth and heaven is, he can surely be no gentleman'?
questions.explanation: Russell quotes this as characteristic of James's warm, democratic, anti-snobbish religious temperament.

questions.prompt: Compare William James's and George Santayana's attitudes toward religion, as Russell presents them.
questions.answer: James was a heretical Protestant who believed good conduct mattered most and, out of democratic feeling, could not accept one truth for philosophers and another for ordinary people; he regarded Santayana's stance as immoral. Santayana, a 'Catholic free-thinker,' liked religion aesthetically and historically rather than as a guide to moral life, did not intellectually accept Christian dogmas, but was content that others believe them and appreciated what he saw as the Christian myth.
questions.explanation: Russell frames this as a lasting temperamental opposition between Protestant and Catholic sensibilities that persists even among the unorthodox.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Russell's probability-based objection to James's Will to Believe.
questions.answer: James's argument seems to grant an equal right to believe any of several undecided hypotheses. But James never considers probability, which is almost always discoverable. If, for instance, a Chinese observer faces Confucianism, Buddhism, and Christianity, and it is granted that at most one can be true, then even giving two of them an even chance implies the third is more likely false than true -- so the 'equal right to believe any of them' collapses once probability is admitted.
questions.explanation: This is one of Russell's central technical objections to the Will to Believe, alongside his objection that James ignores degrees of belief short of full belief or disbelief.

questions.prompt: According to James, what are the two coequal precepts that make up the duty of veracity?
questions.answer: 'Believe truth' and 'shun error.' James argues the sceptic wrongly attends only to the second, causing them to miss out on believing various truths.
questions.explanation: This is the foundation of the Will to Believe argument.

questions.prompt: How does Russell's own account of truth differ from James's pragmatist account?
questions.answer: Russell holds that a belief about a past occurrence is true, or as nearly true as possible, in virtue of a certain relation to its causes (e.g., a real historical event). James holds that a belief is true insofar as it has good effects. Russell argues this reverses the natural order of explanation: we call 'Columbus existed' true because of the real man who lived 450 years ago, not because of the consequences of believing it.
questions.explanation: Russell develops this contrast using the Santa Claus and Columbus examples to show James's account can make useful falsehoods 'true.'

questions.prompt: What is Russell's single main disagreement with James's radical empiricism, apart from his objections to the Will to Believe and pragmatism?
questions.answer: Russell disputes James's use of the word 'experience' for the world's single underlying stuff, since common sense holds that things occur (e.g., unobserved events) without being experienced; Russell proposes instead that an event is 'experienced' when it sets up a habit, and habits require life, so 'experience' is not coextensive with all of reality.
questions.explanation: This is Russell's one substantive qualification of an otherwise strongly endorsed doctrine.

quiz.explanation: Russell opens the chapter with James's dates, 1842-1910.

quiz.prompt: What does James call the single underlying 'stuff' of radical empiricism?
quiz.explanation: James defines 'pure experience' as the immediate flux of life underlying both knower and known.

quiz.prompt: The doctrine that the world's basic stuff is neither mind nor matter, drawn as an implication of James's radical empiricism, is called:
quiz.explanation: James's followers, though not James himself, drew out 'neutral monism' from radical empiricism.

quiz.prompt: According to James's Will to Believe, the duty of veracity consists of which two coequal precepts?
options: Doubt everything; believe nothing without proof
quiz.explanation: James held these two precepts equal in weight, which Russell argues leads to a permissive licence to believe.

quiz.prompt: Russell agrees with James's use of the word 'experience' to describe the single stuff that composes the entire world, including events no living thing ever notices.
quiz.explanation: Russell disagrees here: he holds experience requires life and habit-formation, and is therefore not coextensive with everything that exists.

quiz.prompt: What is Russell's main objection to James's claim that a belief is 'true' if it has good effects?
